newsitem.title: UK: AIDS "guinea pigs" deserve drugs for life - experts.
newsitem.headline: AIDS "guinea pigs" deserve drugs for life - experts.

text.p: Companies that test AIDS drugs on patients in poor countries should offer them free treatment even after the trials are over, researchers said on Friday.
A series of commentaries in the British Medical Journal argued that developing countries should not been seen as a source of cheap human guinea pigs.

"In any medical study, every patient...should be assured of the best possible diagnosis and therapeutic methods," wrote Sean Emery and David Coooper of the University of New South Wales in Sydney. Doctors should be free to use any measures that can save lives or alleviate suffering, they added.
"In our view these explicit statements demand the continued provision of antiretroviral therapy," they wrote.
"Clinical research in countries of the developing world must not be seen solely as a cost-saving mechanism."

Peter Cleaton-Jones of South Africa's Committee for Research on Human Subjects said he understood that large multinational companies were attracted to do research in countries like his, where an average of 7.5 percent of women attending antenatal clinics were infected.
But what happens when a trial ends?
"If a patient infected with HIV responds to the test drugs, may one ethically withhold the drugs at the end of the trial?" he asked.
"My committee's opinion up to the present has been that it is not ethical to do so and that such trial subjects must continue to receive the antiretroviral treatment after the trial ends," he added.
"Naturally, most companies have not received this opinion with joy." He said ethics committees should ensure that volunteers are not exploited.

Peter Busse, of South Africa's National Association of Persons With AIDS, said HIV-infected people had a right to a voice in their own treatment. Unless they had one, they would be suspicious of the drugs companies' intentions.

Peter King of Roche Products in Britain said the key to resolving such disputes was communication. Without saying whether drugs companies should continue treatment, he said patients needed to understand the medical issues.
"The way forward is to forge alliances," he said, noting that companies like his that made AIDS drugs were working with patient advocacy groups.
